aldemar.headline: Intel prices $20 billion of dilution into a falling tape — and Gabriel's stop was touched
aldemar.standfirst: Tuesday was the third red day in a row: the S&P fell 0.74% to 7,693.12 and the Nasdaq gave up 1.3% as chipmakers sold off again, this time with Intel at the centre — a follow-on share offering upsized to $20 billion priced at $95, a 6.5% discount, and the stock closed −6.57% at 96.69 after printing a 95.25 low that traded through Gabriel's 95.52 stop. The 30-year yield held above 5.3%, its highest since 2007, Brent held above $90, and Home Depot's clean beat was ignored. The war impasse is now simply the backdrop: no talks scheduled, no extension sought, oil carrying the risk.

positions.title: 1 signal on INTC — read before the open (BAC quiet)

items.html: INTC — Intel upsizes its follow-on to $20B at $95 a share — the stock closes −6.57% and Gabriel's stop traded. More than 210 million new shares priced at a 6.5% discount is real dilution funding the foundry build-out, and the market charged for it the way it has charged every AI balance-sheet story this month. Tuesday's low of 95.25 went through Gabriel's stop at 95.52: if that order was live, he is flat at roughly −1R (about −$20) and the system did its job — say so and INTC comes out of his book. If it was a mental stop, the edition's own rule applies: holding past the stop is what turns a 1R loss into the kind that ruins expectancy — at 96.69 the position is −8.4% on entry at −0.88R with the stop 1.2% below. Aldemar's position is a different animal by design: −8.6% on entry but only −0.37R against his 81.10 stop, which sits 16.1% below — the full-cycle thesis is intact and the $95 offer price is now the level institutions own it at.

INTC — Analyst target trims to an average $112.20 on EPS dilution. Mechanical re-marks that follow the share count, not new information about demand — the BofA CPU-inference thesis was not touched. The number that matters is $95, where the new stock cleared.

BAC — BAC +0.53% to 64.23 — green again on a red tape, second day running. The relative-strength pattern continues: on Monday it outperformed a falling market, on Tuesday it rose into one, with the 30-year above 5.3% doing the work. Gabriel is −0.23% on entry at −0.04R; Aldemar +0.11% at +0.02R. The 65 rejection from Monday still stands as the ceiling; Home Depot's beat is a small point for the consumer-credit side of the thesis, with Walmart and Target still to come.

positions.note: Signal changes the thesis, the levels or the size — earnings, a regulator with teeth, M&A, a ruling with a revenue line attached. Everything else is filed as noise on purpose; a real signal survives skepticism.

themes.title: Day two without a framework — the impasse hardens into the market's baseline

items.html: No channel reopens: Trump stands on "not in a hurry", Tehran on "no decision to restart". Twenty-four hours after the memorandum lapsed, neither side has moved toward the other and no mediator has a mandate — Monday's threat against Oman saw to that. The market is now pricing an open-ended standoff rather than a delayed deal.

Brent holds above $90 at 90.71; WTI adds 0.40% to 84.84, a fourth straight gain. The premium is no longer event-driven — it is the new resting level. From here the transmission into CPI is mechanical, and it is the reason the regime call refuses to die.

The 30-year holds above 5.3%, the 10-year pushes toward 4.75%. The bond market's verdict on a war with no end date and the deficits that fund it. This is the same force lifting BAC and squeezing everything long-duration — one trade, two sides, both in the book.

themes.note: The transmission is oil → inflation → the regime call, and it is now running in one direction. CPI y/y stands at 3.3 against the 2.5 floor; crude at these levels holds that gate open indefinitely, and Policy tightening — five weeks old — gets another lease. The thing to watch has changed: with no negotiation calendar left, the next repricing comes either from a headline nobody schedules (a strike, a tanker, a back-channel) or from Friday's OPEX unpinning a tape that dealer gamma has been holding still. Watch the tape's character after Friday, not the news wire.

world.title: Third red day: chips pay for their financing again while Home Depot's beat goes unrewarded

items.html: Semis lead the decline again — Nvidia, Broadcom, Micron off 2–7%, CoreWeave −8.3%, Teradyne −8%. Intel's $20B raise gave the AI-financing audit its biggest single exhibit yet, and the whole complex was re-marked. Three weeks ago dilution for datacenters was growth; this week it is cost. That regime change in sentiment is the story of August.

Home Depot beats — EPS $4.92 vs $4.73, revenue $47.9B — and the tape shrugs. A clean beat from the first big retailer after the retail-sales miss, and it could not lift the market. When good earnings stop mattering, the tape is telling you what it is worried about, and it is not earnings. Walmart and Target complete the consumer picture this week.

S&P −0.74% to 7,693.12, Nasdaq −1.3%, Dow −0.22% — the record is now 1.4% above. Three consecutive declines with breadth held up by energy and value while growth pays the yield toll. Orderly so far — but Friday's OPEX removes the dealer-gamma pin that has kept it orderly, and the levels reset Monday.

weekly.headline: The week the market started auditing the AI bill — and the war stopped pretending
weekly.standfirst: Five sessions, a third straight weekly gain, and a record close on Thursday: the S&P added 0.36% to 7,785.76 while the VIX fell to 14.25. Underneath that calm, two things changed. Investors began pricing how AI infrastructure is financed rather than what it might earn — Alphabet on Tuesday, Broadcom and Applied Materials on Friday — while the CPU side of the same trade got re-rated upward. And the war moved from rhetoric to enforcement: a US helicopter disabled a tanker running the blockade, Hormuz traffic sank to three-month lows, and the interim deal now expires on Tuesday.

Two inflation prints cooled, one consumer cracked, and the AI trade split in half

TECHThe AI capex audit begins: GOOG −3.6% Tuesday on a $25bn bond deal, AVGO −6% Friday on a $370bn financing question. Alphabet's quarterly capex hit $44.9bn with free cash flow negative for the first time; Broadcom was marked down on how a lease-and-debt structure gets funded. The market spent this week deciding that the cost of the build belongs in the valuation.TradingKey · Yahoo Finance · 11–14 Aug
SEMISBofA lifts the 2030 CPU market from $170bn to $210bn — INTC ran 6.3% Thursday before fading 2.0% Friday. Vivek Arya's argument is that AI moving from training to inference resets the GPU-to-CPU ratio toward 1:1. It is the bull case for both INTC positions, and Friday showed it will not travel in a straight line.Motley Fool · BofA · 13 Aug
DATACPI cooled Wednesday, PPI cooled Thursday to 4.7% from 5.5%, then retail sales fell 0.6% Friday. Three prints that moved September from a coin flip to a hold. The tone changed midweek: the first two were disinflation, the third was demand weakening — the same direction with a very different meaning for earnings.BLS · AP · 12–14 Aug
RATESThe 30-year auction clears at 5.216% — the highest in a quarter century. The long end refused to follow the cooler prints down, which is a fiscal and energy verdict rather than a policy one. It is the single cleanest reason to be long a bank here.Yahoo Finance · 14 Aug
NOISEFiled and ignored: Pixel 11 previews, an Alphabet 11-year retrospective, a $107.66 Intel target already overtaken. A week's worth of commentary that arrived after the moves it described. None of it touched a thesis, a level or a size.various · 10–14 Aug

The through-line is that this market has stopped paying for AI ambition and started pricing AI arithmetic — who is writing the cheques versus who is cashing them. You now hold one of each: Alphabet writing them, Intel cashing them.

From rhetoric to Hellfire missiles in five sessions

STRIKEA US Navy helicopter disables the M/V Vela Nova with two Hellfire missiles in the Gulf of Oman. The first commercial vessel fired on since the ceasefire, and the moment the blockade stopped being a declaration. Engine room and steering gear, deliberately disabling rather than sinking.12 Aug
SHIPPINGHormuz traffic falls to near three-month lows as both sides claim control. Trump says the strait is open under US control; Iran says nothing passes without its permission. The traffic data settles it — whoever is right, the tankers are not sailing.13 Aug
MILITARYHegseth: the blockade can hold "indefinitely"; a relief carrier group sails Friday. Words backed by a rotation schedule. The market's hope that enforcement fades on its own was removed this week.13–14 Aug
OILWTI rose 4.7% on the week to 81.84 while equities made a record. Energy finished as the week's best sector. Crude is carrying the war risk that the equity indices are not.10–14 Aug

The week's arc runs from talks-are-close on Monday to a missile strike on Tuesday to annexation talk on Friday. Nothing was signed, and the June interim deal now expires on Tuesday 18 August with the blockade live and both sides demanding compensation from the other.
